outcome: Nothing in the window settles or moves the classical question. No classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm has appeared, and no accepted proof that factoring is outside P has appeared either. In-window events are: an unrefereed 2024 preprint claiming factoring is not in P; conditional or subexponential factoring methods (2024, 2025); quantum resource and correctness results (quantum only); a withdrawn quantum claim about LWE, which is not factoring; a 2025 preprint claiming a sqrt(n) method, which is not polynomial in the bit length; and 2026 GNFS engineering records (RSA-260 by Cognition using its Devin agent; RSA-896 by Steve Weis using Claude) whose authors say they do not improve the algorithm.
problem_asks: Can integer factorization be done in polynomial time? Parts: (1) Is there an algorithm that, given any positive integer N with n bits, outputs its prime factorization (or a nontrivial factor when N is composite) in time polynomial in n, on every input? (2) The statement names no machine model and no randomisation. Read literally it asks the unqualified question. The usual reading in the field is classical (non-quantum) computation, so the classical case is the one the bullet is taken to ask. The quantum case is a separate question with a positive answer (Shor, 1994), recorded below as an event. (3) The decision version (does N have a factor in a given range?) is part of the same question, because the search and decision versions are polynomially related.

events.what_happened: Peter W. Shor, polynomial-time randomised algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms on a hypothetical quantum computer. Per the arXiv comments field, the first version appeared in the Proceedings of the 35th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (Santa Fe, 20–22 Nov 1994). The arXiv version quant-ph/9508027 (v1 30 Aug 1995, withdrawn; v2 25 Jan 1996, current) is an expanded version. Journal reference SIAM J. Sci. Statist. Comput. 26 (1997) 1484. Opened the arXiv abstract page; did not read the full text.
events.revisions: arXiv quant-ph/9508027: v1 30 Aug 1995 (withdrawn); v2 25 Jan 1996 (current). Journal: SIAM J. Sci. Statist. Comput. 26 (1997) 1484.
events.delivers: A randomised polynomial-time factoring algorithm, but only on a quantum computer (Shor's model); also covers discrete logarithms. Answers the question affirmatively for quantum computation and says nothing about classical computation.
events.remains: Whether factoring can be done in polynomial time on a classical machine, which is the unqualified question as the field usually reads it.

events.what_happened: Yuly Shipilevsky, 'Integer Factorization is in P' (Optimization Online, posted 31 Aug 2012, updated 7 Apr 2014). The landing-page abstract claims 'a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorization, wherein integer factorization is reduced to solution of a convex polynomial-time integer maximization problem'. The page mentions no verification, acceptance, erratum or withdrawal. Opened the landing page; did not open the PDF.
events.revisions: Posted 31 Aug 2012; updated 7 Apr 2014 (the page describes no change).
events.delivers: If correct, a deterministic polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm, which would answer the bullet affirmatively for classical computation. Not checked by anyone I found.
events.remains: Everything, unless the reduction is valid and the optimisation subproblem is polynomial in general.
events.doubts: (a) No review, endorsement or refutation found in my searches. (b) A search snippet of De Loera, Hemmecke, Onn, Rothblum and Weismantel says convex integer maximization is intractable even for fixed d, since it contains linear integer programming, which is NP-hard for d=1. The reduction would therefore have to avoid the general problem. I did not open that paper. (c) A search snippet says the PDF abstract reads 'minimization', while the landing page reads 'maximization'. I did not open the PDF to resolve this. (d) A 2012 Lipton post titled 'How not to prove integer factoring is in P' appeared in one search; I could not open it or confirm that it concerns this paper.
events.direction: Claims yes for classical computation, if correct. No accepted support found.

events.what_happened: Oded Regev, 'An Efficient Quantum Factoring Algorithm' (arXiv:2308.06572). Abstract: circuits of Õ(n^{3/2}) gates, run about √n+4 times, followed by polynomial-time classical post-processing with lattice reduction. Correctness relies on a number-theoretic heuristic assumption. Opened the arXiv abstract page; the heuristic statement is in the full text, which I did not read.

events.remains: Unconditional correctness (addressed by Pilatte, 2024); the classical question.

checked_by.what_they_did: Proved a version of the heuristic number-theoretic conjecture, so Regev's algorithm and later variants are unconditionally correct

events.doubts: Correctness was conditional on a heuristic; the condition was removed by Pilatte (2024). Regev's own abstract says it is 'currently not clear' whether the algorithm improves physical implementations.

events.what_happened: Rama Garimella, 'Integer Factorization Is Not in P: Logical Proof' (EasyChair Preprint 12579). Version 1 dated 18 Mar 2024; version 2 dated 1 Jul 2024, which adds a subsection 'Towards determination of NP COMPLETENESS of INTEGER FACTORIZATION PROBLEM'. Abstract, as fetched: using Ramanujan's theorem, 'the unique factorization of Highly Composite Number cannot be performed using a polynomial time algorithm'; because the class of Highly Composite Numbers is countably infinite, 'integer factorization is NOT in class P'. Opened the EasyChair landing page and versions page.
events.revisions: v1 18 Mar 2024 (EasyChair 12579); v2 1 Jul 2024 (adds NP-completeness subsection).
events.delivers: Claims a negative answer for general integer factorization (not in P). The derivation shown concerns only the highly composite numbers. The abstract as fetched reaches the general conclusion from that subfamily and from countability.
events.remains: All of the bullet. The argument as summarised does not reach general integers.
events.doubts: (a) The argument as summarised concerns only highly composite numbers. The abstract and landing page show no step from that subfamily to arbitrary integers. (b) Countability of a class is not, on its face, a complexity-theoretic property. (c) The page gives Ramanujan's theorem only as the basis of the claim; the theorem and the application are not stated. (d) Not peer reviewed; EasyChair preprints are not refereed. (e) A search snippet lists a Mahindra University (Hyderabad) affiliation; the EasyChair page I opened lists no affiliation. (f) Version 2 adds a subsection 'Towards determination of NP COMPLETENESS', which, per a search snippet, treats NP-completeness as not yet determined; the main claim about P is unaffected by that subsection.
events.direction: Claims a negative answer, cutting against polynomial-time factoring. Unvetted.

If it holds, the exponent for univariate polynomial factorization over finite fields improves, and the best deterministic exponential-time exponent for integer factorization falls from 1/5 to 1/6. The post says: 'my Devins built the world's highest-performance GPU lattice siever' and 'Devin otherwise autonomously handled measurements, cluster operations, and optimization end-to-end'. events.what_happened: The manuscript 'Exact quantum factoring over a fixed finite gate set' (OpenAI, dated 25 September 2026; the only manuscript in this family) claims a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits that, for every integer N ≥ 2, outputs the complete prime factorization of N (primes in nondecreasing order with multiplicity) with probability exactly one (Theorem 1 in the introduction; abstract). Gate count and qubit count are bounded by a fixed polynomial in n = max{128, ⌊log₂N⌋+1}. The gate set is NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, S = diag(1,i), their inverses and their singly controlled versions. The construction has four parts. (a) An order trial (Proposition 'order-trial') replaces the Fourier phases of Shor's order sampling by a piecewise-linear phase register and adds classical correction modes. It returns either no candidate or a multiple of the order r of a mod m, and the probability that it returns exactly r is φ(r)λ(r), with λ(d) = 2^(−⌈log₂d⌉−10). (b) A recursive process (Proposition 'process') factors N and, recursively, p−1 for each odd prime factor p. Primes are checked by a deterministic polynomial-time test (Lemma 'primality', an AKS-type variant proved in the appendix). Composites are split by gcd(a^(r/2)−1, m) using orders found by the trial. It uses K = n⁵ repetitions per transition and L = n¹⁰ transition slots. (c) Deferred filters applied after the data have been generated (Lemma 'completion', Proposition 'known-probability') make the success probability of the whole preparation exactly p* = (1−2⁻ⁿ)^(n¹⁰) > 1/2. (d) A further dyadic correction gives a preparation whose success flag has probability exactly 1/4 (Lemma 'quarter'). One exact reflection step at that known probability, which the proof of the theorem carries out itself, then yields the factorization with certainty. The manuscript states that it 'makes no claim of a classical deterministic or randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm'.
events.delivers: In the quantum circuit model with classical basis inputs, the claim gives the exact, zero-error, worst-case version of the quantum case: a uniform, polynomial-size family of quantum circuits over one fixed finite gate set that outputs the full factorization with probability one, with no repetition, no bounded-error guarantee and no supplied advice. It strengthens Shor's bounded-error polynomial-time quantum factoring, which the introduction cites. Restrictions: the bounds are polynomial in n with no explicit degree stated, and the body's parameters are large (L = n¹⁰ slots, K = n⁵ repetitions per transition, phase grid Q = B¹⁶ with B = 2ⁿ). The introduction says these are not intended as practical resource improvements. The result is about quantum circuits only. The manuscript's statement of the problem ('the nondecreasing list of primes whose product is N, including multiplicities') matches the list's 'outputs its prime factorization'. The manuscript does not restate the list's classical question and does not claim to settle it.
events.remains: If the claim holds, the classical question is untouched: whether a classical deterministic or randomized algorithm can factor N in time polynomial in log N, and the classical decision version. Also left open within the quantum model: the degree of the polynomial bounds and any practical resource count.

machine_checked.scope: The formalization constructs a polynomial-time uniform quantum circuit family that outputs the complete prime factorization of every integer $N\ge2$ with probability exactly one. The circuits use one fixed finite set of bounded-arity gates, and both the gate count and number of qubits have polynomial worst-case bounds in the bit length of $N$. The probability-one conclusion is exact, rather than an asymptotic or bounded-error guarantee.

events.doubts: (1) The identification of the implemented acceptance event, with deferred filters computed from the generated data, with the analytic event used in the probability calculation (Proposition 'known-probability') is argued in prose. The quantum-implementation step is deferred to Lemma 'records', whose proof is a short sketch ('Induction over the procedure shows that their squared norms ... equal those in the measured procedure'). The introduction calls the deferred-test identification 'the crucial argument'. (2) The primality test (Lemma 'primality') is presented as a variant of AKS. Its correctness proof adapts AKS root-counting lemmas (Lemmas 4.7–4.8 and their footnotes, credited to Lenstra, Macaj, Kalai, Sahai and Sudan), and the constants and auxiliary prime are chosen within the appendix. (3) Uniformity is defined per bit length, but the proofs of Lemma 'quarter' and of the theorem write V_N for each N and speak of 'fixed classical input N'. The text covers this in one sentence (a circuit for a fixed bit length with the input bits as controls is polynomial-time uniform), so the per-N and per-length readings are asserted to coincide rather than separately proved. (4) The polynomial degree is never stated, and the parameters are large (see 'delivers'). The text notes this itself.
events.direction: proves the quantum case exactly (zero error, fixed gate set); classical case not addressed
events.object: The explicit object is the uniform quantum circuit family itself. For each bit length it is a circuit with N in classical basis input bits, generated by a deterministic polynomial-time classical algorithm (Section 2 and the proof of the theorem in Section 6). This is an explicit construction, not an existence argument. Its classical subroutines (the primality test, the factor-tree verification and the classical controller) are compiled into the same gate set. It is not a classical factoring algorithm.

disputes.summary: Opposite claims about the classical question: Shipilevsky (2012) says factoring is in P, and Garimella (2024) says it is not. Neither has accepted support, and they cannot both be right. I record both and do not pick one.

The D-Wave RSA-2048 claim (Wang et al., published 30 Dec 2024) is presented as the first RSA-2048 factorisation by annealing. Press coverage and a commentary say the target was specially structured and easy, so the claim does not reach general RSA moduli.
The RSA-2048 run count in Chevignard, Fouque and Schrottenloher differs between the February 2024 IACR news item (60 runs, snippet) and the current abstract (40 runs on average).

Whether the unqualified bullet asks a classical question. Shor (1994) gives polynomial time on a quantum computer, and the Wikipedia article says factoring is known to be in BQP. A reader who takes the bullet literally could count it as answered for quantum computers. The record treats the classical reading as the question asked, and records the quantum events separately.

The date of the Cognition RSA-260 factorisation: the post says factoring finished 3 Sep 2026 and was written up 9 Sep 2026; a secondary report describes the factorisation as 3 Sep. I dated the event to the write-up, following the first-public-written-argument rule.

summary: The question is open for the classical case, and nothing in the window moved it. I searched for classical polynomial-time claims, quantum and conditional advances, and AI involvement, and opened the primary sources for each event I could reach. The most significant in-window events are: Garimella's 18 March 2024 EasyChair preprint claiming factoring is NOT in P (unrefereed; its derivation covers only highly composite numbers, and I found no visible step from that subfamily to all integers; I found no endorsement or refutation); Murru and Salvatori's September 2024 method, polynomial only given a regulator multiple; Umans and Wang's November 2025 conjecture, which improves the exponent of exponential-time factoring from 1/5 to 1/6 if true; Friedlander's April 2025 sqrt(n) summation claim, which is not polynomial in the bit length; and the quantum results (Pilatte 2024 removing Regev's conditional assumption; Chevignard et al. 2024 qubit reductions; Gidney 2025 resource estimate), none of which speaks to classical complexity. Shor's 1994 quantum algorithm is the only accepted polynomial-time factoring result, and it is quantum. Two 2026 GNFS records carry AI involvement: Cognition's RSA-260 (9 Sep 2026), where the post credits its Devin agent with building the GPU lattice siever and running the cluster, and Weis's RSA-896 (19 Sep 2026), where the write-up says 'Claude was used to port CADO-NFS to run on GPUs' and that it 'orchestrated' the GPU fleet. Both authors say the algorithm was not improved (Cognition: 'I report essentially no algorithmic advancements'; Weis: 'did not meaninfgully [sic] improve the runtime of the General Number Field Sieve'). Under the AI rule, this is engineering around the mathematics rather than mathematics the work would have had to establish otherwise, so I put none in ai.systems and set none_found to false for both. A judging pass may weigh it differently, since both systems wrote and ran the factoring code. Several events are dated from search snippets or fetch summaries and are flagged as such. The Garimella affiliation conflicts: a search snippet lists Mahindra University, but the EasyChair page I opened lists none. The Epoch AI FrontierMath 'Prime Factorization' open problem asks for a better constant in the GNFS exponent, which is not a polynomial-time question; it shows status Unsolved, and I found no solution. The page I opened lists no model evaluations, while a search snippet claimed a table with GPT-5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Deep Think results; I could not reconcile the two and did not record either as an event.
competing_reading: (1) The bullet names no machine model. Read as written, Shor's 1994 result, together with the 2024 unconditional correctness proof (Pilatte) and Wikipedia's note that factoring is in BQP, answers the question affirmatively, so the bullet could be counted as settled in the window's prior history. I record that reading and the classical reading separately. (2) Garimella's claim is a complete negative answer if it is right, which would settle the classical bullet negatively; I found nothing that supports it. (3) The Weis and Cognition events could be read as AI-assisted progress on factoring, since the systems wrote and ran the factoring code, and the RSA-896 record is the largest public RSA challenge number factored after the RSA-260 record. Both authors say the mathematics is unchanged, so this reading treats engineering as the substantive development, which the rule in DEEP_DIVE 5.4 does not count.
what_would_settle_it: For the classical question: a refereed proof of a polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm, or of a superpolynomial lower bound (or non-membership in P), accepted by experts. For the Garimella claim: an expert reading that either closes the step from highly composite numbers to all integers or identifies the gap. For the Shipilevsky claim: a refereed evaluation of the reduction to convex integer maximization. For the quantum reading: a decision by the judging pass on whether the bullet means classical computation. For the AI events: a source from the authors giving the substance of the contribution (not only engineering), or a claim that the algorithm was changed.

judgement.why: The statement is read as the classical question, the standard meaning of 'can integer factorization be done in polynomial time' as an open problem; quantum polynomial time has been known since 1994, so every quantum result (Shor, Regev and its successors, Pilatte, resource estimates, and the OpenAI exact-quantum-factoring manuscript, which itself disclaims any classical result) is a variant. Conditional or oracle-aided algorithms (Agrawal–Saxena–Srivastava, Morain–Renault–Smith, Murru–Salvatori, Umans–Wang) and reductions (Hittmeir) are variants or none, as they do not deliver unconditional polynomial time or a lower bound. The GNFS records factor single numbers by an existing method and bound nothing; their AI involvement was engineering, with no system in ai.systems, so none. The two whole-scope claims (Shipilevsky yes, Garimella no) are set aside as not_credible: each claims a landmark result with years of silence, and each has a visible structural flaw (an NP-hard subproblem; a general lower bound inferred from a trivially factorable subfamily). The OpenAI event is answered generated on the README quote, though the quote is repository-wide rather than specific to this manuscript.
judgement.doubts: If the statement were read literally (no machine model), Shor 1994 would answer it pre-snapshot and the problem would be open_stale; this verdict takes the classical reading. The OpenAI ai_basis quote covers 'the vast majority of results' in the repository, not this manuscript by name. Garimella not_credible rests on the abstract's argument as summarised; the body was not read.
